description: Bulalakaw is a team of students from the Polytechnic University of the Philippines (PUP).
summary:
Bulalakaw Station is a browser-based Mars outpost survival game built in Godot by Team Bulalakaw from the Polytechnic University of the Philippines.

You play as the Night Commander watching over four crewmates through seven Martian nights. Instead of fighting monsters, you manage real mission problems: stretching battery power until sunrise, scrubbing CO2, keeping crops alive, repairing broken hardware, and waiting through real Earth-Mars radio delays. Every night draws from actual NASA mission records—including the 2018 global dust storm, the September 2017 solar particle event, and the May 2024 X12 solar flare—alongside live solar flare updates from NASA's DONKI API.

Space weather and radiation risks are easy to overlook when they are only numbers in a report. By turning real mission data into quick, hands-on decisions, Bulalakaw Station helps players understand what it actually takes to keep a crew alive on Mars.
details:
Our Goal

Space STEM content for children often falls into one of two traps: either it presents passive trivia without decision-making, or it buries students in spreadsheets they cannot parse. As challenge author Mike Given framed it, a junior astronaut trainer should be "not a quiz, not a slideshow, a living simulation where every choice costs something." Our goal is to bridge that gap by making real NASA planetary science approachable, interactive, and emotionally engaging—showing young learners that surviving on Mars depends on understanding interconnected systems rather than memorizing isolated facts.

What Bulalakaw Station Does

Bulalakaw Station puts young players in the commander's seat of a Martian habitat in Gale Crater for seven nights until the supply ship arrives, leading a four-person astronaut crew (Lani, Maya, Mateo, and Carlo). Instead of fictional monsters, the challenge comes from real, interconnected Martian physics:

  • Thermal Management: Turning the Heater down during a -70°C Martian night saves battery but slows crew movement, increases camera sensor noise, and spoils crop growth if left on LOW for more than 60 seconds.
  • Atmosphere Control: Running Life Support (MOXIE) on LOW conserves power, but lets CO₂ build up and O₂ drop toward emergency mask levels.
  • Power-Capped Surveillance: Watching CCTV Cameras is the only way to spot physical sparks, answer crew requests, collect nightly NASA Science Discoveries, and log clues for the Malfunction Detective Board—but each active camera drains 0.04%/s of battery, and only two can be powered at once.
  • Solar Storm Response: When a Solar Particle Storm triggers on Sky Radar, light arrives first—giving a 20-second warning window to Recall EVA Crew (R) through the airlock and Close the Storm Shelter Door (Space) (reducing radiation dose transmission from 20% to 10% to 5%) before energetic protons hit the surface.
  • Deep Space Communications: Tapping ASK EARTH (Q) or SEND DISCOVERY (T) sends radio waves across the Deep Space Network with a realistic one-way light-time delay (3 to 22 minutes, scaled 5 seconds per real minute in-game). If a dust storm, dish drift, or Night 7's 04:00 solar blackout drops signal quality below 5% mid-transmission, the packet is lost.

How It Works

Each Martian day (sol) follows a two-phase architecture that connects daytime preparation with nighttime survival:

1. Daytime Base Hub

During the day, players walk the Commander across Gale Crater using keyboard or touch controls to upgrade seven station facilities across three levels—the Solar Field, Battery Bank, MOXIE Life Support, Greenhouse, Storm Shelter, Suit Bay, and Comms Dish—using Materials earned from surviving night shifts.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

Figure 2. Base Hub

Before the Control Room opens each night, players must step inside every unlocked facility to complete a mandatory hands-on learning gate. Each visit unlocks a daily NASA Lesson Card (39 lessons total) featuring a two-sentence plain-language explanation, an explicit honesty badge (Real NASA Data vs. Simplified), an authentic NASA mission photograph, and a real-number bar chart. From Night 2 onward, players can also accept optional space-kid sponsor deals that grant extra materials per night at the cost of pop-up posters covering one camera monitor until tapped closed.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

Figure 3. NASA Lesson Card/Building Info Pop-up

2. Nighttime Command Desk

During each night shift, players operate a 180-second real-time simulation (representing 18:00 to 06:00 on Mars) where every station system interacts dynamically. The Command Desk continuously tracks stored battery power alongside a live end-of-night forecast arrow, oxygen levels, individual crew radiation doses measured in chest X-rays, food stores, crew morale, and communications link quality.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

Figure 4. Night Desk

Each night also conceals one hidden station malfunction from three possible causes. Players act as detectives by watching the camera feeds to log clues weighted by sensor reliability, spending battery power to scan specific rooms, and diagnosing the root fault before systems fail.

Whenever sparking hazards appear on the security feeds, tapping them launches one of seven tactile 10 to 20 second repair minigames. Players fix the station by reconnecting keyed wires, brushing dust off solar panels, sealing airlock leaks, tightening greenhouse pipes, packing regolith shelter bags, or re-aiming the Earth dish, with each completed repair concluding with a verified NASA science fact.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

Figure 5. Night Desk | Hazard Minigame/s

Project Benefits

By combining a forgiving "Rough Night" rule, where low oxygen or high radiation triggers emergency masks rather than an instant game-over, with “Calm Mode”, a 17-step practice tutorial, and progressive hint arrows, the game allows children to test risky decisions and learn from consequences without frustration. Pairing real NASA mission photography with clear "Real NASA Data" versus "Simplified" honesty badges, a post-shift debrief panel, and a 9-entry Space Codex also builds early scientific literacy, helping young players distinguish authentic space measurements from simplified game mechanics.

Tools and Technologies Used

  • Game Engine & Languages: Godot Engine 4.7.2 (GDScript) for 2D game development, exported to HTML5/WebGL2 for zero-install browser play.
  • Art & Asset Pipeline: Original character sprites, camera feeds, base map, and UI layouts drawn by our team, processed into 2× pixel art with 1 px outlines using Python (Pillow).

    DOCS LINK: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1H0Dyi0_kezhYWXtCyR6XVIpOTD4DbFInaerAT5rGMis/edit?usp=sharing

Play Bulalakaw Station (Live Web Demo) You can play the full game directly in your browser with no installation required at

https://bulalakaw-spaceapps-hackathon.github.io/Integration/

First-time players can start with the interactive Tutorial on the title screen, and judges who are short on time can click Judge Mode to jump straight into any night or explore the full mission with all upgrades unlocked.

The source code and assets for our project are also available on our team GitHub organization at
